displayTable: Model Framework
Conductance Formulation
Parameter Identifiability
Required Observations
Model Limitations
Steady-State, Linear Conductance
Constant K_{\text{plant}}:$$\Delta\Psi = \frac{E}{K_{\text{plant}}}$$Flow is linearly proportional to the water-potential gradient via Ohm's law analogy.
High (Deterministic): Single parameter (K_{\text{plant}} or R_{\text{total}}) is uniquely identifiable from the linear slope of \Delta\Psi versus E.
• Pre-dawn water potential (\Psi_{\text{soil}} \approx \Psi_{\text{pd}})
• Midday leaf water potential (\Psi_{\text{leaf}})
• Transpiration flux (E) at midday plateau
• Neglects capacitive buffering, phase lags, and diurnal hysteresis.
• Fails during severe drought due to omission of xylem cavitation.
• Assumes instantaneous equilibration (dV/dt = 0).
Steady-State, Nonlinear Conductance
Tension-dependent K(\Psi):
Q = \int_{\Psi_{\text{leaf}}}^{\Psi_{\text{soil}}} K(\Psi)\,d\Psi
Incorporates vulnerability curves (e.g., Weibull or sigmoidal functions describing cavitation).
Moderate: High-tension observations are required to constrain the inflection point (P_{50}) and shape parameter (a). Susceptible to equifinality if data are confined to mild water stress.
• Paired \Psi_{\text{soil}}, \Psi_{\text{leaf}}, and steady-state E measured across a broad range of soil drying levels
• Direct benchtop xylem vulnerability curves (centrifuge, acoustic, or air-injection)
• Omits transient capacitive discharge and recharge dynamics.
• Assumes xylem repair or cavitation is instantaneous with shifting potentials.
• Cannot capture morning-versus-afternoon path-dependent responses.
Transient, Linear Conductance

Constant K_{\text{plant}} with constant bulk capacitance C_{\text{leaf}}:$$C_{\text{leaf}}\frac{d\Psi_{\text{leaf}}}{dt} = K_{\text{plant}}(\Psi_{\text{soil}} - \Psi_{\text{leaf}}) - E(t)$$Linear first-order ordinary differential equation.

Moderate: The relaxation time scale \tau = C_{\text{leaf}}/K_{\text{plant}} is identifiable from phase shifts, but individual separation of C_{\text{leaf}} and K_{\text{plant}} requires independent volume or flux data.
• Continuous high-frequency diurnal E(t) (sap-flow or gas exchange)
• Continuous or high-frequency stem/leaf \Psi(t) (stem psychrometry)
• Baseline pre-dawn \Psi_{\text{soil}}
• Fails beyond the turgor loss point, where tissue capacitance shifts.
• Does not capture runaway cavitation or stomatal closure safety margins.
• Overestimates flow rates under extreme midday water potentials.
Transient, Nonlinear Conductance & Capacitance

Coupled state-dependent functions K(\Psi) and C(\Psi):$$C(\Psi_{\text{leaf}})\frac{d\Psi_{\text{leaf}}}{dt} = Q_{\text{in}}!\left(K(\Psi), \Delta\Psi\right) - E(t)$$Dynamic pressure-volume curves coupled to hydraulic vulnerability.
Low (Ill-Posed without Priors): High risk of equifinality among multiple parameters (e.g., P_{50}, vulnerability slope, osmotic potential at full turgor \pi_0, elastic modulus \varepsilon).
• High-frequency diurnal sap flow at multiple stem heights (to quantify storage discharge)
• Continuous leaf and stem psychrometry
• Leaf pressure-volume (P-V) curves
• Conduit cavitation vulnerability curves
• High parameter sensitivity and experimental burden for calibration.
• Potential numerical stiffness during catastrophic xylem embolism.
• Difficult to generalize across phenological stages or contrasting species.
